title: Delivery-versus-Payment and Payment-versus-Payment Across Ledger Topologies
subtitle: Atomic platforms, synchronization operators and asynchronous hybrid settlement
abstract: Settlement architecture cannot be evaluated solely by whether two smart-contract transfers execute in one block. Financial finality is the enforceable discharge of payment or delivery obligations under the relevant systems and governing law. TSP-01 compares three engineering models: a common atomic platform, a synchronization operator joining independent final systems, and an asynchronous hybrid process with contingencies. Each has different risk allocations, controls and failure modes.

evidence.heading: Shared programmable platform
evidence.body: BIS Project Agorá delivered a prototype combining tokenized commercial-bank deposits with central-bank reserves on a shared programmable wholesale platform. It demonstrates a particular way of coordinating actors and money claims while retaining institutional roles and safeguards. It is not a general guarantee that placing every issuer, security and bank on one chain resolves legal settlement and governance questions.

evidence.heading: Synchronization can preserve existing infrastructure
evidence.body: Project Meridian and Meridian FX explore synchronizing external asset or FX systems with existing real-time gross settlement infrastructure. The core insight is that a coordinator can condition the release of legs on the other leg's state without moving every asset and currency to one ledger. This option requires trusted interfaces, precise finality semantics and procedures for unavailable or inconsistent systems.

evidence.heading: PvP and DvP mitigate but do not erase all risk
evidence.body: BIS analysis of FX settlement risk documents exposure when one currency is delivered irrevocably before the other. DvP similarly attempts to link securities delivery and payment, but counterparty default, market liquidity, operational outage and legal venue rules can remain material. Project Helvetia and Rialto demonstrate experimental settlement options under their own assumptions; generalizing their results to all tokenized assets would be unwarranted.

architecture.heading: Topology A: shared atomic execution
architecture.body: Both delivery and payment representations execute inside one shared transaction boundary under common permission and validator policies. Rollback of an unsuccessful operation may be well defined within that platform, but the platform still needs legal recognition of its asset and money records, issuer authority, bridge/oracle validity and sufficient funds. Off-chain custody and issuer obligations can remain external.

architecture.heading: Topology B: synchronization across separate finality systems
architecture.body: A synchronization operator coordinates reservations, conditional locks, acknowledgments and releases across separate infrastructures—for example a tokenized securities venue and RTGS. It must know when a commitment can still be aborted and when each independent system has achieved irrevocable finality. The coordinator may reduce principal risk while introducing availability, governance and interface dependencies.

architecture.heading: Topology C: asynchronous hybrid with recovery
architecture.body: One leg may travel via a bank rail and the other through a DLT system, with no native cross-system atomicity. Escrow, conditional delivery, liquidity buffers, timeout policies or compensating transactions can mitigate exposure. A reversal of an already-final bank settlement may be legally impossible, so a compensation process may create a new financial obligation instead of undoing the original event.

architecture.heading: What counts as completion
architecture.body: A completed exchange requires matching eligible parties, valid instruction, acceptable instrument and amount, final payment under its rules, final asset delivery and balancing journals. Do not conflate an instruction acknowledgment, tentative blockchain inclusion, RTGS payment acceptance and legally effective discharge. Each timestamp must be tied to its originating authority.

case.title: Synthetic USD 90,000 DvP security exchange
case.setup: A buyer agrees to acquire a permitted tokenized security entitlement for USD 90,000. The asset is on a token registry and the cash is either represented on the same platform or sent through an external bank.
rows: Validate asset and payment → apply both or neither
Platform atomicity; legal finality requires governing rules
Exposure interval, escrow or compensation required
Evidence links payment, claim and journal
case.formula: PvP principal exposure is bounded by the amount irrevocably delivered on one leg without the other; synchronized settlement aims to reduce that interval but does not set every legal risk to zero.
case.interpretation: Identical economic obligations can be fulfilled through distinct technical architectures with different operational and legal assurances. A 'one-click' user experience need not imply atomic financial finality.

risks: Asset delivered but payment fails or vice versa.
Conditional release, legal escrow and defined recovery process.
A synchronized transaction remains locked because an operator becomes unavailable.
Timeout governance, safe abort/continue states and independent evidence.
A bridge reports a bank settlement that is not legally final.
Authenticated source verification and explicit finality semantics.
tests: Implement one exchange in all three topologies; classify every failure by whether none, one or both legs are final.
Measure peak prefunding, unreconciled positions and time-to-spendable funds without inventing performance benefits.
Inject coordinator restarts, delayed confirmation and duplicate callbacks, then prove no double delivery or double payment.
conclusion: SPE and RPI should compare settlement topologies with a common legal and accounting specification. The best architecture is the one that delivers provable discharge and recoverable exceptions for the actual institutions—not simply the fewest ledger transactions.

title: Accounting-Driven Settlement: Claims, Discharge and Independent Verification
subtitle: Why financial-state completeness matters more than a valid transaction hash
abstract: Settlement protocols need to reconcile legal obligations, instruction validity, final money transfers and independent accounts. A payment event can be cryptographically valid while failing to discharge the full contractual claim or overlooking a disputed liability. This report develops a claims-based settlement ledger that tracks authorized obligations, partial discharge, assigned creditors and independently reconstructed balances.

evidence.heading: Financial market infrastructure is a system of obligations
evidence.body: The BIS/CPMI tokenisation report and IMF studies highlight why programmable financial arrangements must account for rights, money and infrastructure governance. Project Agorá and Meridian demonstrate different coordination approaches but neither eliminates the need for clear obligation identity and finality. The economic ledger must define which buyer owes what to which holder, not infer all receivables from wallet balances.

evidence.heading: Token supply cannot establish accounting completeness
evidence.body: On-chain transfer and burn logs describe a known population of events, not necessarily every creditor, customer deposit or off-chain asset right. FSB analysis warns of complex interdependencies in tokenized financial arrangements. Auditors need to reconcile independently sourced contracts and bank records to the token ledger. A system can be internally balanced and still omit an entire class of liabilities.

evidence.heading: Governance and exceptions are part of finality
evidence.body: Account assignment, contract modification, payment netting and dispute resolution can change obligation quantities without immediate money movement. A network receiving two authenticated approvals cannot assume the newer instruction revokes the older one unless that relationship is formally defined. Recording policy versions, signers, counterparties and transaction IDs is essential to enforce release and replay rules.

architecture.heading: Canonical obligation model
architecture.body: Represent each enforceable claim as ClaimID, underlying contract, debtor, creditor or beneficial holder, amount, currency, eligibility, status, assignments and maturity, linked to evidence. Separate issued claims from disputes and conditional payments. A verified payment instruction identifies the specific obligations and proportions it is authorized to discharge. This allows the same buyer obligation to be assigned among supplier, financier or multiple investors without fabricating extra principal.

architecture.heading: Accounting consistency across distinct actors
architecture.body: An economic settlement should generate matching counterparty entries under each institution's accounting policy, not necessarily one shared general ledger. At a simplified claim level, ApprovedOutstanding_before = ApprovedOutstanding_after + FinalSettledAmount, subject to amendments or cancellations. For every credit transfer, the sender's discharged payable should correspond to recipient claims and independently evidenced final funds; differences remain explicit exceptions.

architecture.heading: Authorize, execute, prove and reconcile
architecture.body: First authenticate principals and check amount, limits, consent and replay nonce. Then execute through chosen rail, collect appropriate finality proof, recognize payment discharge and update token or entitlement state. Finally reconcile claim register, token ledger and bank/payments journal. Ordering is intentional: a provisional bank acknowledgment or transient blockchain inclusion should not trigger irreversible legal discharge without an agreed rule.

architecture.heading: Completeness is an external assertion
architecture.body: A valid zero balance does not prove that no other invoices or claims were omitted. Assurance must include supplier statements, contract population, custody backing inventory, issuance approvals and payment-provider statements, with gaps recorded. The audit should reconstruct positions from independently controlled evidence and verify policy exception handling, rather than rely solely on the operator's own event feed.

case.title: Synthetic multi-holder partial settlement of a USD 100,000 invoice
case.setup: A buyer owes USD 100,000 under a contract. After verification, USD 90,000 is approved and USD 10,000 remains disputed. Approved rights are allocated 60% to supplier and 40% to a financing institution.
rows: Creditors sum to the same $90,000 obligation
case.formula: ApprovedOutstanding = 90,000 − FinalSettled. After first installment = $60,000. Creditor allocation: supplier 60% and financier 40% of each approved payment; disputed $10,000 accounted separately.
case.interpretation: No new principal arises when the approved claim is assigned. The legal assignment, the token allocation and the monetary settlement are three linked but different events.

risks: Duplicate callback produces two token burns or two outgoing bank transfers.
Stable payment IDs, nonce verification and idempotency.
Payment is complete to one holder but the other holder's assigned amount is missing.
Population completeness and entitlement sum checks.
Settlement ledger marks paid on receipt of non-final network status.
Defined finality proof and provisional states.
tests: Prove accounting identities for approved, outstanding, settled, assigned and disputed claims under partial settlement and netting.
Inject one missing claim and demand that external statement reconciliation detects a population gap.
Compare journal balancing under atomic ledger transfer, RTGS synchronization and delayed bank wire, including compensation.
conclusion: Accounting-driven settlement is a richer research target than fast token movement. SPE, TRR and RPI can implement a common obligation and evidence protocol that makes incomplete financial state detectable and allows controlled recovery after cross-rail failure.
